question:
Patient note:
A 21-year-old man in his third year of an aeronautical-engineering program presented to the university’s combined pulmonary–rheumatology clinic this morning at the request of his primary practitioner for an updated assessment before he spends a semester working on wind-tunnel experiments at 2 400 m elevation. He reports that since childhood he has relied on twice-daily inhaled budesonide-formoterol, a bedtime montelukast tablet, and a salbutamol metered-dose inhaler that he empties every three weeks; despite this regimen he continues to wheeze with cold air and develops chest tightness after jogging more than one kilometre, and an office spirometry performed last month recorded an FEV1 of 1.82 L (56 % predicted) with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.61 that improved by only 7 % after 400 µg salbutamol, findings unchanged from the prior two years and interpreted as fixed airflow limitation. He has never required intubation but was admitted twice to the paediatric intensive-care unit for status episodes before age ten, and over the past twelve months he has completed three tapers of oral prednisone, the most recent six weeks ago during a viral upper-respiratory infection. Oxygen saturation today is 96 % on ambient air at rest and falls to 91 % after four flights of clinic stairs, at which point his respiratory rate climbs to 24 breaths/min with audible end-expiratory wheeze that resolves after two salbutamol puffs. In parallel with his airway disease he has lived for six years with a symmetrical polyarthritis that began with morning stiffness in the metacarpophalangeal and proximal-interphalangeal joints; laboratory work at that time revealed a rheumatoid-factor titre of 1:160 and anti-cyclic-citrullinated peptide antibodies above 200 U/mL, and a hand radiograph last year showed mild periarticular osteopenia without erosions. He self-injects methotrexate 25 mg subcutaneously every Friday night, supplements with folic acid 1 mg daily, and receives adalimumab 40 mg every other week; the most recent Disease Activity Score documented by rheumatology was 2.8. Joint discomfort remains low enough that he rides a fold-up bicycle across campus, though he avoids pull-ups because of persistent shoulder pain after a lacrosse injury. Endocrine records indicate that at age eleven capillary glucoses in the high 200s led to institution of a basal–bolus insulin program; he now wears a continuous subcutaneous pump delivering degludec basal rates between 0.8 and 1.1 U/hour with aspart correction boluses calculated by a 1:10 carbohydrate ratio. Finger-stick logs e-mailed yesterday show pre-breakfast values ranging 95–165 mg/dL, and last month’s glycated haemoglobin measured 7.2 %. He denies blurred vision, paresthesias, foot ulcers, orthostatic dizziness, or episodes of severe hypoglycaemia, and a retinal photograph obtained six months ago was normal; a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio drawn at the same visit read 19 mg/g. He has never experienced crushing substernal pressure, diaphoresis with exertion, calf cramping, transient facial droop, speech arrest, or unilateral weakness. He reports no history of myocardial infarction, stroke, transient ischemic attack, peripheral vascular disease, peptic or duodenal ulcer disease, chronic liver disease, solid-organ or hematologic malignancy, human immunodeficiency virus infection, hemiparesis, or cognitive impairment. He was born at 30 weeks’ gestation, spent two months in neonatal intensive care for bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and never smoked; recreational cannabis is used twice a year, and he drinks two craft beers on weekend evenings but abstains while on methotrexate. Family history reveals a father with long-standing psoriatic arthritis treated with biologics and an older sister who carries an albuterol inhaler for exercise-induced symptoms; there is no premature coronary disease or cerebrovascular event in first-degree relatives. Current medications include the inhaled steroid–long-acting bronchodilator combination, salbutamol as outlined, montelukast 10 mg nightly, methotrexate, adalimumab, insulin via pump, cyanocobalamin 1 000 µg monthly for marginal levels noted last year, and vitamin D3 2 000 IU daily; he developed urticaria to trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole as a child and avoids that antibiotic class. At 09 : 20 vital signs were temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg in the right arm, heart rate 86 beats/min regular, respirations 18 breaths/min at rest, and oxygen saturation 96 % on room air; weight 69 kg and height 180 cm yield a body-mass index of 21.3 kg/m². He sat upright, conversing in full sentences, with faint perioral cyanosis appearing only after the stair test described above. Conjunctivae are pink, sclerae anicteric. Neck is supple with brisk carotid up-strokes, no bruits, and jugular venous pulsation 2 cm above the sternal angle at 45°. Cardiac examination discloses a nondisplaced point of maximal impulse, a regular rhythm with physiologic splitting of S2, no murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lung percussion is hyper-resonant bilaterally; auscultation detects diffuse end-expiratory wheezes and prolonged expiration, but no crackles. Abdomen is flat and nontender with normal bowel sounds, liver span percusses 10 cm in the mid-clavicular line, edge non-palpable, and no splenomegaly or ascites are appreciated. Hands exhibit mild ulnar deviation at the second metacarpophalangeal joints and trace effusion of both wrists without warmth or erythema; grip strength is 4/5 bilaterally, and he achieves full extension of elbows and knees against resistance. Lower extremities show brisk dorsalis pedis pulses, no edema, and intact sensation to monofilament and vibration at halluces. Neurologic screening reveals orientation to person, place, and date, intact cranial nerves II–XII, symmetric 5/5 strength in proximal and distal muscle groups, normal heel-to-shin coordination, and a steady gait once his breathlessness subsides. Laboratory results drawn on arrival demonstrate sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 3.9 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 11 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, fasting glucose 142 mg/dL, total bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 22 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 24 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 78 U/L, albumin 4.5 g/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.0; complete blood count shows haemoglobin 14.2 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 86 fL, white-blood-cell count 6.8 × 10⁹/L, and platelet count 268 × 10⁹/L. A 12-lead electrocardiogram reveals normal sinus rhythm at 84 beats/min, PR interval 150 ms, QRS duration 92 ms, axis 10°, and no ST-segment deviation. Portable postero-anterior chest radiograph depicts hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms and mild peribronchial thickening but normal cardiac silhouette. The patient seeks guidance on whether his current inhaler plan will suffice at altitude, how to schedule methotrexate dosing around planned vaccinations for overseas travel, and the safest strategy for adjusting basal insulin during anticipated hikes on weekends in the mountains.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) sums weights for qualifying chronic conditions; the age-adjusted version also adds points starting at age 50.
- Age: 21 years → 0.
- Chronic pulmonary disease: Persistent symptomatic airflow limitation requiring daily inhaled therapy, with FEV1 56% predicted → 1.
- Rheumatic disease: Seropositive rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate and adalimumab → 1.
- Diabetes without documented end-organ damage: Insulin-treated diabetes with no evidence of retinopathy, nephropathy, or neuropathy → 1. Insulin use alone does not qualify as end-organ damage.
- Other qualifying CCI conditions: None documented → 0.
Total = 0 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 3.
Final answer: 3
